sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events E0–E3493. Annotation uses the retained text only; apparent transcription errors, missing slide content, and events containing both speakers limit precision. U marks inseparably mixed events, including substantive speech joined to housekeeping. No edited teaser replay was identifiable.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: there is no Injustice unless there's Justice and there is no justice unless God exists
candidates.explanation: The formula moves from justified outrage to God's existence and redirects suffering toward confirmation. E920–925 supply a transcendent-standard argument, and E950–977 explain the good/evil dependency; these are real reasons, though they do not establish why the standard must be God. Whether the formula replaces that disputed premise remains uncertain.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: laws come from lawgivers where does the law of gravity come from
candidates.explanation: The maxim supplies the bridge from regular physical behavior to a personal legislator without explaining why descriptive natural laws require enactment. E1020–1143 develop a related argument about directed processes, and E1173 repeats the maxim, but neither distinguishes physical regularities from prescribed rules. No device expressly excludes criticism.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: science can't demonstrate that God doesn't exist
candidates.explanation: The mechanic/Ford analogy distinguishes an originating agent from an operating mechanism, so this is a supplied argument. Its categorical wording may exclude scientific counterevidence, but the immediate target is the inference from successful mechanism explanations to God's nonexistence. It is unclear whether E1557–1562 exclude probabilistic evidence as well as disproof.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: moral objections don't disprove God they require God to exist
candidates.explanation: The formula redirects suffering objections into evidence for their target by invoking God's alleged necessity for objective value. That dependency was argued at E914–983, although challenged at E1235–1261. E1631 explicitly concedes possible evidence for naturalism, and E1650 makes restoration conditional, preventing a confident finding that every adverse pattern is neutralized.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: any experiment he tries to run in order to show that materialism's true has to assume materialism's false
candidates.explanation: E1675–1693 categorically disqualify any neuroscience result supporting materialism: if successful, its investigator's reasoning becomes untrustworthy. This is explicit protection through a self-defeat argument, not merely lack of a falsifier. The argument supplies its determinism premise, previously developed at E716–759; its disputed validity does not make it an unsupported slogan.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: we can only speculate here but it could be to encourage a longer search
candidates.explanation: Possible hidden purposes explain delayed belief through maturity, later conversions, or reduced culpability. These could insulate hiddenness from evidence if unrestricted, but E1695 expressly calls them speculation and E1698–1708 offers limited possibilities rather than declaring all nonbelief explained. The passage does not clearly establish a merits-independent dismissal.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: but if he gave me his wisdom too I would leave things as they are
candidates.explanation: E1717–1735 reserve judgment about apparently gratuitous suffering to an omniscient perspective, invoking untraceable future benefits. The adopted maxim upgrades possible hidden goods into approval of the world unchanged without establishing adequate justification for every case. E1631's earlier concession qualifies the broader speech, but this episode expressly neutralizes contrary appearances through inaccessible wisdom.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: the only way you could know is if the immaterial does exist
candidates.explanation: Responding to Lowder's hypothetical, Turek makes knowledge itself conditional on the immaterial, excluding a knowledgeable materialist regardless of findings. E2154–2160 supply his mind/free-will rationale, so this is a protected argument rather than a slogan. Lowder's mechanism/reliability distinction at E2085–2101 and E2110–2137 remains directly relevant to its disputed premise.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: most moral disagreements originate in willful denial
candidates.explanation: Against moral disagreement as counterevidence, Turek attributes most disagreement to knowingly suppressing inconvenient truth. That discounts disagreement through the dissenter's motives without assessing its merits. E3397–3399 includes himself, and 'most' limits the scope; nevertheless, the broad motive attribution supplies explicit protection. It is an explanatory claim, not a compact slogan replacing argument.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.explanation: The theft formula portrays Lowder's probabilistic reasoning as dependent on the view it opposes. E3413–3428 assert divine grounding, while earlier teleology arguments provide some rationale. Lowder expressly offers autonomous abstract objects at E3233–3254. It is uncertain whether this renewed use supplies only a disputed explanation or substitutes the accusation for addressing that alternative.

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: I'm not going to stand up here on stage and say that this has the same thing going for it
contrasts.explanation: Lowder identifies reported partial support for an RNA-world account while explicitly distinguishing its standing from established physics. E2341 corrects his RNA/DNA slip, and E2350–2358 further qualifies his confidence. This is a tentative evidential answer, not a settled affirmation replacing reasons.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: we haven't proven the Christian God by just these arguments you have to go further
contrasts.explanation: Turek explicitly limits the conclusion of his presented arguments and identifies additional historical evidence needed for Christianity. E2635–2637 corrects his necessary/sufficient terminology. The qualification prevents his generic-theism case from automatically serving as proof of a particular religion.
